My father has been waiting over 18 weeks for an MRI scan. I contacted the surgery out of serious concern, particularly as he had already been sent directly to the hospital on appointment by this very GP due to dangerously high blood pressure which triggered this whole experience. While in hospital, doctors discovered he had also suffered a heart attack, and he was admitted for further care.

This is especially alarming given that only a few weeks prior, my mother—also under this practice’s care—tragically passed away from a heart attack. One would expect heightened vigilance and compassion in light of this family history, especially with an ongoing, unexplained delay in crucial diagnostic imaging.

When I reached out, I was told by a receptionist to complete an eConsult on his behalf which I did. I was assured that an appointment would be made for my father to see doctor aktar, instead he received a dismissive written response stating uncertainty about whether they could help or refer him for an MRI, with no follow-up call, no attempt to discuss the matter further, and no offer of support or alternative solutions. But they could see an appointment with the hospital for the 20th. (Talk to them) Exactly words. News to my father..no such correspondence has been sent and no such letter for an appointment has been received.

This response falls far short of the GP’s duty of care. General practitioners are responsible for advocating for their patients' health, especially in urgent or deteriorating cases. They should coordinate with secondary care services, provide clear communication, and ensure vulnerable patients are not left in limbo.
